questions.question_text:
A committee of $3$ members is chosen at random from $5$ men and $5$ women.
What is the probability that the committee consists of $2$ men and $1$ woman?

options.why: Assumed an even split of genders has probability 1/2 without evaluating the combination counts.
Calculated $\frac{\binom{5}{2} \times \binom{5}{1}}{^{10}P_{3}} = \frac{50}{720}$, mixing combinations in numerator with permutations in denominator.
Calculated $\frac{\binom{5}{2}}{120}$, forgetting to multiply by $\binom{5}{1}$ for the woman.

questions.question_text:
$6$ students line up at random in a row.
What is the probability that $2$ specific students, Liam and Emma, do NOT stand next to each other?

options.why: Calculated the probability that Liam and Emma ARE together instead of not together.
Forgot the internal permutation $2!$ of Liam and Emma when finding the complement.
Assumed adjacent and separated outcomes are equally likely.

questions.solution_text:
Total arrangements: $6! = 720$
Liam and Emma together: $5! \times 2! = 240$
$P(\text{together}) = \frac{240}{720} = \frac{1}{3}$
$P(\text{not together}) = 1 - \frac{1}{3}$
$= \frac{2}{3}$

questions.question_text:
$2$ cards are drawn at random without replacement from a standard deck of $52$ cards.
What is the probability that both cards are Kings?

options.why: Counted the $4 \times 3 = 12$ ORDERED King pairs but divided by the UNORDERED total $\binom{52}{2} = 1326$, giving $12/1326 = 2/221$.
Treated the draw as WITH replacement, so $(4/52)^2 = (1/13)^2 = 1/169$.
Made both slips at once: assumed replacement AND doubled for the two orders, giving $2 \times (1/13)^2 = 2/169$.

questions.solution_text:
Total ways to draw $2$ cards: $\binom{52}{2} = 1326$
Ways to draw $2$ Kings: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$
$P(\text{both Kings}) = \frac{6}{1326}$
$= \frac{1}{221}$

questions.question_text:
A $3$-digit number is formed by randomly arranging $3$ distinct digits from $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}$.
What is the probability that the resulting number is odd?

options.why: Answered the complement: counted the $4$ EVEN units digits, $4 \times {}^{5}P_{2} = 80$, so $80/120 = 2/3$.
Allowed only the digit $1$ as an odd units digit and overlooked $3$, giving $1 \times 20 = 20$ and $20/120 = 1/6$.
Overlooked $3$ as odd AND answered the complement, treating $5$ of the digits as even: $5 \times 20 = 100$, so $100/120 = 5/6$.

questions.solution_text:
Total $3$-digit numbers: $^{6}P_{3} = 120$
Odd digits $\{1, 3\}$ ($2$ choices for units digit).
First $2$ digits: $^{5}P_{2} = 20$
Favourable numbers: $2 \times 20 = 40$
$P(\text{odd}) = \frac{40}{120}$
$= \frac{1}{3}$

questions.question_text:
A bag contains $7$ red marbles and $3$ blue marbles.
If $3$ marbles are drawn at random without replacement, what is the probability of drawing at least one blue marble?

options.why: Found the probability of drawing zero blue marbles (the complement) without subtracting from 1.
Calculated probability with replacement as $1 - (7/10)^3 = 1 - 343/1000 = 657/1000$.
Used the single-draw proportion $3/10$ rather than evaluating the 3-marble selection.

questions.solution_text:
Total selections: $\binom{10}{3} = 120$
No blue marbles (all $3$ red): $\binom{7}{3} = 35$
$P(\text{no blue}) = \frac{35}{120} = \frac{7}{24}$
$P(\text{at least } 1 \text{ blue}) = 1 - \frac{7}{24}$
$= \frac{17}{24}$

questions.question_text:
$5$ people sit at random around a circular table.
What is the probability that $2$ designated people sit next to each other?

options.why: Forgot the internal arrangements $2!$ of the two designated people.
Used linear seating $(4! \times 2!)/5! = 2/5$ instead of circular seating.
Used $(5-1)!$ as denominator but subtracted 2 from the numerator unit count incorrectly.

questions.solution_text:
Total circular arrangements: $(5-1)! = 4! = 24$
Designated pair together: $(4-1)! \times 2! = 3! \times 2 = 12$
$P(\text{together}) = \frac{12}{24}$
$= \frac{1}{2}$

questions.question_text:
A council of $5$ is selected at random from $6$ Conservatives and $4$ Labour members.
What is the probability that Conservatives hold a majority on the council?

options.why: Only counted the case with exactly 3 Conservatives ($120/252 = 10/21$), omitting 4 and 5.
Assumed majority probability is 1/2 without evaluating the unequal group sizes.
Omitted the all-Conservative case ($180/252 = 5/7$).

questions.solution_text:
Total selections: $\binom{10}{5} = 252$
Case 1 ($3$ Cons, $2$ Lab): $\binom{6}{3} \times \binom{4}{2} = 20 \times 6 = 120$
Case 2 ($4$ Cons, $1$ Lab): $\binom{6}{4} \times \binom{4}{1} = 15 \times 4 = 60$
Case 3 ($5$ Cons, $0$ Lab): $\binom{6}{5} \times \binom{4}{0} = 6 \times 1 = 6$
Favourable: $120 + 60 + 6 = 186$
$P(\text{majority}) = \frac{186}{252}$
$= \frac{31}{42}$

questions.question_text:
$5$ cards are dealt at random from a standard deck of $52$ cards.
What is the probability that all $5$ cards are of the same suit?

options.why: Calculated the probability for one specific suit without multiplying by 4 for the 4 suits.
Calculated $\frac{\binom{13}{5}}{\binom{52}{5}} \times 13$ incorrectly.
Calculated $(1/4)^5$ assuming independent suit draws with replacement.

questions.solution_text:
Total hands: $\binom{52}{5} = 2598960$
Choose suit: $\binom{4}{1} = 4$
Choose $5$ cards of that suit: $\binom{13}{5} = 1287$
Favourable hands: $4 \times 1287 = 5148$
$P(\text{all same suit}) = \frac{5148}{2598960}$
$= \frac{33}{16660}$

questions.question_text:
$3$ Maths books, $2$ Physics books, and $3$ Chemistry books are arranged randomly in a row on a shelf.
What is the probability that books of the same subject stay together in their respective subject blocks?

options.why: Forgot to multiply by $3! = 6$ for the arrangement of the 3 subject blocks.
Forgot the internal arrangement of the Physics books ($2!$).
Multiplied by $3 \times 3 = 9$ instead of $3!$ for the block order.

questions.solution_text:
Total arrangements: $8! = 40320$
Arrange $3$ subject units: $3! = 6$
Internal arrangements: Maths $3! = 6$, Physics $2! = 2$, Chemistry $3! = 6$
Favourable: $6 \times (6 \times 2 \times 6) = 432$
$P(\text{blocks together}) = \frac{432}{40320}$
$= \frac{3}{280}$
